primary.key: Therefore, for the perfect man who is unavoidably summoned to power over his fellows, there is naught like Inaction.
primary.s: After eight refinements the world cherishes in error, the chapter turns to the ruler; Guo Xiang, on chapter 11, reads inaction not as folded hands and silence but as leaving each thing to act of itself, so that nature and life are at rest.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 13, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907032 (2026)

basis.words: 無為者，非拱默之謂也，直各任其自為，則性命安矣。
basis.gloss: [On 故君子不得已而臨蒞天下，莫若無為:] Inaction does not mean folding the hands and keeping silent; it is simply leaving each to act of itself, and then nature and life are at rest.

standby.key: “Of old, the Yellow Emperor first caused charity and duty to one’s neighbour to interfere with the natural goodness of the heart of man.
standby.s: Lao Tzŭ, asked how to order hearts, turns to history; Guo Xiang, on chapter 11, reads the disturbing as done by the traces of a ruler merely one with things, never aiming at charity and duty, traces to which later hearts gave themselves up.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 13, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907032 (2026)

basis.words: 夫黃帝非為仁義也，直與物冥…迹自見，則後世之心必自殉之，是亦黃帝之迹使物攖也。
basis.gloss: [On 昔者黃帝始以仁義攖人之心:] The Yellow Emperor did not practise charity and duty; he was simply one with things (and so their traces appeared of themselves). … Once the traces appeared, the hearts of later ages were bound to give themselves up to them; so it is the Yellow Emperor’s traces, too, that set things in turmoil.

primary.key: “Let all things revert to their original constitution. If they do this, without knowledge, the result will be a simple purity which they will never lose; but knowledge will bring with it a divergence therefrom.
primary.s: Pressed again, the Vital Principle tells the Spirit of the Clouds to rest in inaction; Guo Xiang, on chapter 11, reads the return as true only when made without knowing, for things left in chaos to return of themselves never leave their root.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 13, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 7907032 (2026)

basis.words: 不知而復，乃真復也。…渾沌無知而任其自復，乃能終身不離其本也。…知而復之，與復乖矣。
basis.gloss: [On 各復其根而不知:] To return without knowing is true return. … [On 渾渾沌沌，終身不離:] In undivided chaos, knowing nothing and left to return of themselves, they can all their lives not leave their root. … [On 若彼知之，乃是離之:] To return by knowing is at odds with returning.

standby.key: “To act by means of inaction is God. To speak by means of inaction is Virtue.
standby.s: Following the Master’s saying on the Way, the text lists ten points; Guo Xiang, on chapter 12, reads the first two as a doing and a speaking not undertaken, which do and speak of themselves: the Way of heaven and true virtue.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 14, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356578 (2026)

basis.words: 不為此為，而此為自為，乃天道。…不為此言，而此言自言，乃真德。
basis.gloss: [On 無為為之之謂天:] Not doing this doing, and yet this doing does itself: that is the Way of heaven. … [On 無為言之之謂德:] Not speaking this speech, and yet this speech speaks itself: that is true virtue.

primary.key: When ONE came into existence, there was ONE, but it was formless. When things got that by which they came into existence, it was called their virtue.
primary.s: A brief account of the beginning moves from the Nameless toward destiny, form and nature; Guo Xiang, on chapter 12, reads it as things getting life of themselves, since non-being cannot produce them, and virtue as leaving them to that self-getting.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 14, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356578 (2026)

basis.words: 夫一之所起，起於至一，非起於無也。…夫無不能生物，而云物得以生，乃所以明物生之自得，任其自得，斯可謂德也。
basis.gloss: [On 一之所起，有一而未形:] The arising of the One arises from the utmost One, not from non-being. … [On 物得以生，謂之德:] Non-being cannot produce things; the text says things got that by which they live to make clear that the life of things is got of themselves, and to leave them to that self-getting is what may be called virtue.

standby.key: He strives to do no wrong; but he is ignorant of the source from which wrong springs.
standby.s: Hsü Yu judges Yeh Ch’üeh unfit to be emperor; Guo Xiang, on chapter 12, reads wrong as arising from cleverness and knowing, so that forbidding it by knowing deepens it, and freedom from it lies in putting knowing away, not in forbidding by force.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 14, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356578 (2026)

basis.words: 夫過生於聰知，而又役知以禁之，其過彌甚矣。故曰，無過在去知，不在於強禁。
basis.gloss: [On 彼審乎禁過，而不知過之所由生:] Wrong is born of cleverness and knowing; to set knowing to work again to forbid it makes the wrong all the greater. Hence it is said: to be without wrong lies in putting knowing away, not in forcible prohibition.

primary.key: But Confucius said, “That fellow pretends to a knowledge of the science of the ante-mundane. He knows something, but not much. His government is of the internal, not of the external.
primary.s: Tzŭ Kung tells Confucius of the gardener who scorned machines; Guo Xiang, on chapter 12, reads the pretence as lying in his turning from the present to the past, ashamed of the world’s affairs, whereas one truly of that art governs nothing, inner or outer.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 14, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356578 (2026)

basis.words: 以其背今向古，羞為世事，故知其非真渾沌也。…夫真渾沌，都不治也，豈以其內為異而偏有所治哉。
basis.gloss: [On 彼假脩渾沌氏之術者也:] Because he turns his back on the present and faces the past, ashamed to take part in the world’s affairs, it is known that he is not the true Hundun. … [On 治其內，而不治其外:] The true Hundun governs nothing at all; how would it set the inner apart and govern that alone?

standby.key: The repose of the Sage is not what the world calls repose. His repose is the result of his mental attitude. All creation could not disturb his equilibrium: hence his repose.
standby.s: The chapter turns from three ceaseless Ways to the Sage’s repose; Guo Xiang, on chapter 13, reads it as stillness not held because it is judged good, which would at times give way to movement, but stillness that nothing can trouble, found in himself.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 13, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 15, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356924 (2026)

basis.words: 善之乃靜，則有時而動也。…斯乃自得也。
basis.gloss: [On 聖人之靜也，非曰靜也善，故靜也:] If he were still because he judged stillness good, there would be times when he moved. … [On 萬物無足以鐃心者，故靜也:] This is finding it in himself.

primary.key: Rulers must practise inaction in order to administer the empire. The ruled must practise action in order to subserve the interests of the empire. This is an unchangeable law.
primary.s: Having praised inaction, the chapter divides ruler from ruled; Guo Xiang, on chapter 13, reads the ruler’s use of the empire as a doing called inaction because it follows his nature, so that, each following his own, no one above or below acts.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 13, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 15, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356924 (2026)

basis.words: 夫用天下者，亦有用之為耳。然自得此為，率性而動，故謂之無為也。…然各用其性而天機玄發，則古今上下無為，誰有為也。
basis.gloss: [On 上必無為而用天下，下必有為為天下用，此不易之道也:] The one who uses the empire also has the doing of using. But because he finds this doing in himself and moves by following his nature, it is called non-action. … But when each uses his own nature and the workings of heaven issue darkly forth, then past and present, above and below, are all non-action: who is it that acts?

standby.key: Is not your elimination of self a positive manifestation of self?
standby.s: Lao Tzŭ retorts to Confucius, who defines charity and duty as universal love without self; Guo Xiang, on chapter 13, reads what the world calls selflessness as setting oneself aside to love others, which, since the lover wants love in return, is deeply selfish.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 13, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 15, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6356924 (2026)

basis.words: 世所謂無私者，釋己而愛人。夫愛人者，欲人之愛己，此乃甚私，非忘公而公也。
basis.gloss: [On 無私焉，乃私也:] What the world calls selflessness is to set oneself aside and love others. But one who loves others wants others to love him: this is extreme selfishness, not the public spirit that comes of forgetting public spirit.

primary.key: “The sky turns round; the earth stands still; sun and moon pursue one another. Who causes this? Who directs this?
primary.s: A new chapter opens with questions about the motions of sky, clouds and wind; Guo Xiang, on chapter 14, reads the sky as moving, the earth as resting and sun and moon as taking turns, each of itself, with no one causing or directing them.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 16, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6365115 (2026)

basis.words: 不運而自行也。…不處而自止也。…不爭所而自代謝也。…皆自爾。
basis.gloss: [On 天其運乎:] It is not turned; it moves of itself. … [On 地其處乎:] It is not set in place; it stays of itself. … [On 日月其爭於所乎:] They do not contend for their places; they succeed one another of themselves. … [On 孰主張是？孰維綱是:] All are so of themselves.

standby.key: “Perfect charity,” said Chuang Tzŭ, “does not admit of love for the individual.”
standby.s: Tang, told that tigers and wolves have charity, asks about perfect charity; Guo Xiang, on chapter 14, reads the lack of love not as coldness but as the body’s, whose head, feet, organs and skin keep their places with no love between them.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 16, the Zhengtong Daozang edition), revision 6365115 (2026)

basis.words: 無親者，非薄惡之謂也。夫人之體，非有親也；而首自在上，足自處下，府藏居內，皮毛在外…於其體中各任其極，而未有親愛於其間也。
basis.gloss: [On 至仁無親:] To be without affection does not mean coldness or aversion. The human body has no affection within it; yet the head is above of itself, the feet below of themselves, the organs within, skin and hair without … within the body each is left to its utmost, and there is no love among them.
